passage: Before my civil-services interview I promised the goddess I would fast every Tuesday for a year if I got in. My sister Yamini watched me skip lunch for a week and said, "Ramesh, you can pray and still eat." I snapped at her. Looking back, I think I was bargaining because the fear was too big to hold otherwise, and I don't call the prayer foolish. I also practised mock questions with her until midnight, which I count as part of the bargain now. The result came in June: no. I sat on the terrace, angry, thinking I hadn't fasted enough. Yamini brought tea and said nothing clever. Weeks later I understood the no was not a verdict on me. I kept the Tuesdays, lighter, for myself, and signed up for the next attempt.

qa.q: What did Ramesh promise the goddess before the interview?
qa.a: Ramesh promised to fast every Tuesday for a year if Ramesh got in.

qa.q: Why does Ramesh think the bargaining happened?
qa.a: Ramesh felt the fear was too big to hold otherwise, so the promise gave it somewhere to go, and Ramesh does not call the prayer foolish.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do beyond the promise, and what does that add?
qa.a: Ramesh practised mock questions with Yamini until midnight and signed up for the next attempt, which shows honest effort still matters alongside faith.

qa.q: How might Yamini have seen Ramesh's fasting?
qa.a: Yamini seems worried, since Yamini told Ramesh to pray and still eat, and later brought tea without clever advice, offering company instead.

grounding: Ramesh bargains with the goddess with a fast for an interview outcome, holds it lightly after a no, and treats the result as not a verdict on worth.

passage: At the fair week of the village temple, Charu handed out prasad and steel cups of buttermilk from the back of the hall. She had done it for three years and liked how the day fell into a rhythm. This year the committee head, Lavanya, announced that each volunteer family should give a fixed sum for the new gate, and that donors' names would be read out on the loudspeaker. Charu did the sums in her head: her father's tailoring shop had had a slow winter. She said quietly, "Lavanya akka, I can give my hours, but not that amount." Lavanya frowned, then softened. "Then give hours. Wash the vessels with the boys." Later a family from the next village, not regulars, hesitated at the door. Charu waved them in and pressed a cup into the mother's hand.

qa.q: What did the committee head announce for each volunteer family?
qa.a: Lavanya announced that each volunteer family should give a fixed sum for the new gate, and that donors' names would be read out on the loudspeaker.

qa.q: What was Charu worried about when she did the sums in her head?
qa.a: Charu worried about affording the fixed sum, since her father's tailoring shop had a slow winter, and did not want to be pushed beyond her means.

qa.q: How did Charu handle the pressure to give?
qa.a: She calmly offered her hours instead of the sum, so she could keep serving without going beyond her means.

qa.q: How might the family from the next village feel when X
qa.a: Possibly welcomed and relieved, since the service seems meant to be open to everyone.

grounding: Charu finds meaning in serving at the temple, gives time rather than the pressured sum, and welcomes strangers.

passage: In the lobby of the accounts firm, a man in a creased shirt caught Hemant by the elbow: his wallet had been stolen, and he needed cash for a bus to Nagpur. Hemant's chest tightened. Only last month a colleague had lost money to a story much like this one. And Hemant could not be sure the man was lying. "I'm sorry, I don't hand out cash," Hemant said, "but I can help another way." Hemant turned to Omkar, the security guard. "Can you call the police help desk and ask what they do for stranded travellers?" Omkar nodded and picked up the phone. Hemant walked to the canteen and came back with a packet of poha and tea. The man took it, said thanks and sat down to wait. Hemant went upstairs unsure whether it was enough, but at peace with it.

qa.q: What did Hemant bring back from the canteen?
qa.a: Hemant brought back a packet of poha and tea.

qa.q: Why did Hemant's chest tighten when the man asked for cash?
qa.a: Hemant remembered a colleague losing money to a similar story, so felt fear of being scammed, though Hemant could not be sure the man was lying.

qa.q: How did Hemant offer help while staying cautious?
qa.a: Hemant declined to hand over cash, asked Omkar to call the police help desk, and bought food and tea instead.

qa.q: How might the man in the creased shirt see Hemant's refusal of cash?
qa.a: He may be disappointed, but the food and the phone call may show him that the refusal was caution, not coldness.

grounding: A stranger asks Hemant for money; Hemant hesitates because of scams, acts on caution, and offers safe help such as a call to the police help desk and food.

passage:
Dear Ujjwal,

I'm not sure you remember me, the one standing beside a dead scooter on the flyover last Thursday, eight in the evening, rain coming, phone almost out of charge. Honestly I was angry at everything: the scooter, the mechanic who had just serviced it, the rain. You stopped your car, checked that I wasn't hurt, and let me charge my phone while you called a tow van for me. You waited until it came. Then you refused any petrol money, so the least I can do is write. The scooter is fixed now. Thank you for giving me your number. I'll pass this on the next time I see someone stuck by the road.

Parveen

qa.q: Where was Parveen when the scooter broke down?
qa.a: Parveen was on the flyover, beside the dead scooter.

qa.q: How was Parveen feeling before Ujjwal stopped?
qa.a: Parveen was angry at everything, including the scooter, the mechanic and the rain, and stuck with a phone almost out of charge.

qa.q: How does Parveen plan to pass the kindness on?
qa.a: By stopping to help the next person seen stuck by the road, as Ujjwal did. 🙂

qa.q: What might Ujjwal have seen at the flyover?
qa.a: A stranger beside a dead scooter with rain coming, who needed a phone charge and a tow van.

grounding: A stranger helps Parveen at a breakdown; Parveen thanks Ujjwal warmly, keeps the contact and plans to pass the kindness on.
